The correct answer is C. The circle of Willis is a series of arterial anastomoses that circle around the pituitary stalk at the
ventral surface of the brain. If any of the vessels of the circle of Willis become blocked, blood can be routed through the
remaining vessels. The abject of this question is to determine which vessel does not belong to the circle of Willis. Of the

Explanation & ReKaps =
The correct answer is B. One large clinical clue is that patient has bilateral symptoms—all four limbs are affected and he has
bilateral Babinski signs. In addition, the patient has awareness and is able to move his eyes vertically and blink The only vessel
listed that can cause bilateral signs and symptoms is the basilar artery, which supplies both sides of the ventral and medial

The angular gyrus (choice A) is located in the dominant inferior parietal lobe. A lesion of this area produces Gerstmann
syndrome, which consists of: 1) agraphia (inability to write}; 2) acalculia (loss of ability to calculate mathematical problems); 3)
right-left disorientation (difficulty identifying right vs. left body parts; 4) finger agnosia (inability to name or identify
individual fingers).
The frontal eye fields (choice B) are in the frontal cortex and are the cortical centers for contralateral horizontal gaze. A lesion
in this area results in an inability to make voluntary eye movements to the contralateral side. Because of the activity of the
intact frontal eye field would be unopposed after this lesion, the result would be a conjugate slow deviation of the eyes
‘toward the lesion ("looks toward the lesion”).
The central sulcus (of Rolando) separates the frontal cortex from the parietal cortex. The precentral gyrus (choice D) is
immediately rostral to this sulcus and is the primary motor cortex in the frontal lobe. A lesion in this area would cause
contralateral upper motor neuron symptoms. (In contrast, the postcentral gyrus is just caudal to this sulcus and is the primary
somatosensory cortex in the parietal lobe )
The prefrontal cortex (choice E) is located in front of (rostral to) the premotor cortex and is where much of one's personality
is located. This area is involved in organizing and planning the intellectual and emotional aspects of beharior. A lesion of this
area produces frontal lobe syndrome, in which patients can have a variety of cognitive, emotional, and behavioral problems.

The anterior tibial artery (choice A), the posterior tibial artery (choice D), and the fibular artery (choice B) are all in
the leg distal to the knee and not typically injured in the posterior location of the knee. The anterior tibial artery and
vein are subject to injury in anterior compartment syndrome in which swelling of the anterior compartment muscles

. 2 abdominal cavity. Below the arcuate line there is no posterior rectus sheath and the rectus abdominis lies directly

. 28 border of the rectus abdominis such that the anterior rectus sheath is formed from the aponeurosis of the
. 29 external oblique and internal oblique, and the posterior rectus sheath is formed from the intemal oblique
- 30 aponeurosis and the transversus abdominis aponeurosis. The transversalis fascia is separated from the

Upon delivery, the baby was notably cyanotic, macrosomic, and 2 8 had relatively poor muscle tone. He was started on 100% oxygen, which improved his oxygen saturation only slightly. After a week of poor feeding and gradually worsening symptoms, the baby eventually 2 - succumbs to his condition. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this baby's death?

The correct answer is E. Maternal diabetes is associated with a number of neonatal complications and congenital anomalies.
Perhaps one of the most well-known complications is neonatal macrosomia (large for gestational age), which may produce a ReKaps
number of issues during delivery. Macrosomia, as seen in this patient, results from hyperinsulinemia (insulin has anabolic functions)
secondary to excessive glucose in the baby’s circulation. Another complication is respiratory distress syndrome, which is thought
to occur as a result of insulin's inhibition of surfactant production. Although this entirely possible in this patient, it is not one of the « Transposition of the great vessels is more
answer choices. commonly seen in infants born to diabetic mothers
An important congenital anomaly associated with matemal diabetes is transposition of the great arteries (TGA). In TGA, the aorta « The aorta emanates from the anterior part of the
takes off from the anterior part of the right ventricle and the pulmonary trunk takes off from the posterior part of the left ventricle (see Tight ventricle and the pulmonary trunk emanates
figure below). This produces a complete separation of the systemic and pulmonary circulations. A shunt of some sort (patent from the posterior part of the left ventricle.
ductus arteriosus, atrial septal defect, or ventricular septal defect) is required for viability, since without such a defect, blood cannot
be oxygenated after returning from the systemic circulation.

Transposition of the great arteries is the most common cyanotic congenital heart defect presenting in the neonatal period,
particularly in diabetic mothers, but remember that truncus arteriosus, tricuspid atresia/stenosis, tetralogy of Fallot, and total
anomalous venous retum (the 5 T's) are also causes of cyanotic congenital heart disease.
Atrioventricular septal defect (choice A), also called AV canal defect or endocardial cushion defect, involves maldevelopment of the
septum at both the atrial and the ventricular levels as well as the tricuspid and mitral valves. It typically does not cause
significant problems until 6 to 8 weeks of age when congestive heart failure can develop. This is commonly seen in Down
syndrome. Reparative surgery is typically done at 4 to 6 months of age.
Coarctation of the aorta (choice B) involves stenosis of a segment of the aorta and occurs in two patterns, adult and infantile. In the
infantile type, the stenosis is proximal to the insertion of the ductus arteriosus (preductal); this patter is associated with
Turner syndrome. These patients may present with heart failure (if severe) and weak distal pulses, but are unlikely to present with
cyanosis, as with this patient. In theadult type, the stenosis is distal to the ductus arteriosus (postductal), and patients
develop collateral circulation of the intercostal arteries. Notching of the ribs can be seen on chest radiographs.
Eisenmenger syndrome (choice C) results when an initially noncyanotic left-to-right shunt (such as an atrial septal defect,
ventricular septal defect, or patent ductus arteriosus) is allowed topersist. The overload of fluid into the pulmonary circulation
results in pulmonary hypertension, which gradually over time produces a right-to-left shunt. This may then lead to cyanosis
since freshly oxygenated blood is mixing with deoxygenated blood prior to entry into the systemic circulation. This commonly
presents months or years later in life.
Tetralogy of Fallot (choice D) consists of a ventricular septal defect, an overriding aorta, pulmonic stenosis, and right
ventricular hypertrophy. It causes cyanosis and is usually diagnosed in infancy. Tetralogy of Fallot is more commonly associated
with DiGeorge syndrome and is not classic for an infant of a diabetic mother.

Defective chemotactic responses (choice B) are seen in many diseases, such as alcoholism and diabetes mellitus.

She has had prenatal care and a first trimester ultrasound had revealed delayed intrauterine growth, microcephaly, cleft palate, and polydactyly. On admission, she delivers a stillborn fetus. The placenta appears normal without infarcts, hemorrhage, or infection. The umbilical cord shows a single umbilical artery. Autopsy examination of the fetus reveals low-set ears, omphalocele, cardiac ventricular septal defect, and Z horseshoe kidney. Polydactyly is noted; hands are not clenched and do not have overlapping fingers. A chromosomal abnormality is suspected. Which of the following features would most likely also be present in this fetus?

stem: A 64-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis comes to the physician because of progressive pain despite treatment with NSAIDs. Treatment with methotrexate is initiated. Over the next 7 weeks, prednisone is also given as a ‘bridging therapy’ to prevent pain and inflammation while waiting for the pharmacologic benefits of methotrexate. Which of the following is a possible adverse effect of the glucocorticoid therapy in this patient?
answer_text: C
explanation: The source identifies hypocalcemia as a possible glucocorticoid adverse effect. Glucocorticoids reduce intestinal calcium absorption and increase renal calcium excretion, lowering circulating ionized calcium and stimulating parathyroid hormone secretion, which can increase bone breakdown. With prolonged use they also cause fluid retention, hypokalemia, hypernatremia, and hyperglycemia. Prednisone is used as bridging therapy because disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs such as methotrexate take weeks to months to work.

Because creatinine is freely filtered at the glomerulus and plasma and urine concentrations are easy to measure, creatinine
clearance is commonly used clinically to estimate GFR. Creatinine is actively secreted by the proximal tubule which
introduces a small error (~10-40%), but changes in Cc, can be a useful indicator of kidney injury and disease. In practice, urine is
collected over a 24 hour period to determine Ug, and urine flow rate. When corrected for body surface area, normal values for GFR
are ~130 and 120 mL/min/1.73 m* for men and women, respectively, although there may be considerable variation with sex and
age even within a single individual.
The blood urea nitrogen concentration (choice A) increases when GFR is reduced.

Run charts (or time plots) (choice D) are graphs of data collected over time that can help determine whether an intervention
or enhancement in the patient care process has resulted in true improvement over time. They can also help to identity if the
intervention simply represents a random fluctuation (that might be incorrectly interpreted as a significant improvement). Run charts
are created by plotting time along the X-axis (e.g. minutes, hours, days, months) and the quality measure on the Y-axis (e.g.
number of infections, wait times, falls). The median (or 50th percentile) is measured using baseline historical data and then
compared to outcomes measured following the quality improvement intervention.
AA Shewhart (or control chart) (choice E) applies formal statistical calculations (statistical process control) to determine whether
the observed rise and fall of a quality measure over time is within a predictable range of variation or is an indication of a
significant change in the system. Control charts use upper and lower control limits (sometimes called “natural process limits”) that
indicate the threshold at which the process output is considered statistically unlikely, and are drawn typically at 3 standard
errors from the center line.
Six Sigma (choice F) is another model for quality improvement with origins from the manufacturing industry. The term comes
from the use in statistics of the Greek Letter (sigma) to denote Standard Deviation from the mean. By definition, 95% of a
normally distributed population falls within 2 standard deviations of the mean average (or "2 sigma"). Hence there are 5% of
observations listed as being "abnormal" or “unacceptable.” Six sigma is equivalent to 3.4 defects (or errors) per million or 6
standard deviations from the population average. This system uses specific steps to reduce variation and improve performance.

stem: A 43-year-old Caucasian man comes to the physician because of gradual hyperpigmentation of his skin. He does not report increased sun exposure and denies use of tanning beds. His past medical history is remarkable for diabetes, which he manages with subcutaneous insulin injections. He does report frequent travel and is frustrated because he always seems to trigger the metal detector at the airport. Which of the following is the most likely underlying explanation for this patient's condition?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. This patient's history is consistent with a diagnosis of hemochromatosis. Hemochromatosis results from
iron overload and can be either hereditary (autosomal recessive) or acquired in patients receiving chronic blood
transfusions (e.g., thalassemia patients) or taking too many oral iron supplements. Our patient likely has the hereditary version of ~
the disease, which results from increased iron absorption from the gut due to genetically impaired detection of circulating iron
levels. It is one of the most common inherited diseases in the Caucasian population. * Hemochromatosis is an iron-storage disorder
characterized by excessive accumulation of iron in
Symptoms of elevated serum iron include micronodular liver cirrhosis (with increased risk of hepatocellular carcinoma), skin body tissues.
pigmentation, pancreatic damage leading to diabetes mellitus ("bronze diabetes”), impotence in males, and congestive
heart failure (due to restrictive or dilated cardiomyopathy). Restrictive cardiomyopathy occurs due to deposition of iron within * It may either be acquired from multiple blood
myocardial cells (causing ventricular diastolic dysfunction), which in severe cases, can progress to dilated cardiomyopathy (causing transfusions or inherited in an autosomal recessive
ventricular systolic dysfunction). These complications are due to damage caused by deposition of iron in tissues; the total body iron pattern. The inherited version results from
in some of these individuals may reach levels large enough to set off some airport metal detectors. Iron studies would show increased absorption of iron from the gut.
increased serum iron, increased transferrin saturation, increased ferritin, and decreased total iron binding capacity.
+ Complications include cirrhosis, increased risk of
Treatment includes phlebotomy and chelation with deferoxamine. hepatocellular carcinoma, skin pigmentation,

stem: A 64-year-old man is admitted to the hospital for treatment of bacterial pneumonia. The treating clinician forgets to ask about allergies and the patient is unaware that his severe allergy to penicillin is not known to the treatment team. The patient receives a dose of intravenous penicillin and suffers an anaphylactic response but is successfully resuscitated by the ‘medical team. Which of the following is the most accurate description of the medical error?

options.text: lip resulting in a near miss
Violation resulting in a near miss
Lapse resulting in an adverse event

explanation:
1. Answer: C. A lapse is an internal event that generally involves a failure
in memory; as opposed to a slip which is an observable action com
monly associated with attentional or perceptional failures resulting in
an unintended execution of a correctly intended action. The result of
the described error was harm to the patient in the form of anaphylaxis
with the need for resuscitation, and therefore is categorized as an adverse:
event. An adverse event is any harm or undesirable clinical outcome
resulting from medical care as opposed to the underlying disease process,
and does not have to result in permanent disability or death. A violation
is a deliberate act of not following policy or procedures, which was not
the situation in this scenario. A near miss is an event or a situation that
does not produce patient harm, but only because of intervening factors or
good fortune. The adverse event described is the result of an error and is
completely preventable.

stem: A 32-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a sore throat, worsening fatigue, and shortness of breath for the past 3 days. She has a history of migraines and has been taking carbamazepine to prevent migraines for many years. Her temperature is 38.6°C (101.5°F), pulse is 100/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 122/70 mm Hg. Physical examination shows several bruises on her legs and arms, conjunctival and oral mucosal pallor, and lungs clear to auscultation. Rectal examination and stool guaiac test are negative. A complete blood count shows an erythrocyte count of 2.0 million/mm³, hemoglobin of 10 g/dL, hematocrit of 30%, and 1,500 white blood cells/mm³. Platelet count is 50,000/mm³. The corrected reticulocyte count is <1%. She undergoes a bone marrow biopsy. Which of the following is the most likely finding on bone marrow biopsy?

options.text: Hypercellularity with megaloblasts and giant metamyelocytes
Marrow hypocellularity, predominance of fat cells and marrow stroma
Ringed sideroblasts on Prussian blue stain

answer_text: C
explanation: The source explains that aplastic anemia presents with pancytopenia and a corrected reticulocyte count below 1%, indicating a poor marrow response. Biopsy typically shows hypocellularity of all cell lines (less than 25% of normal), normal architecture, and predominance of fat and marrow stroma; marrow cellularity varies with age. Causes may be hereditary (e.g., Fanconi anemia) or acquired, including drugs such as carbamazepine, environmental toxins, and viral infections. Treatment may include stopping the causative medication, immunosuppressive therapy, or stem-cell/bone-marrow transplantation. Choice A (giant early red-cell precursors) is associated with pure red-cell aplasia, which selectively affects the erythrocytic lineage. Choice B indicates megaloblastic change from vitamin B12 or folate deficiency. Choice D describes sideroblastic anemia, typically a microcytic anemia. Choice E describes multiple myeloma. The source states that the absence of isolated erythrocytic disease and the involvement of all three cell lines support aplastic anemia.

stem: A 14-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department because of dyspnea, tachycardia, and diaphoresis following a bee sting. A thorough medical history reveals that she has had similar severe responses to bee stings on two other occasions. Which of the following immunoglobulin classes was produced first during the initial response to this antigen?
answer_text: E
explanation: The source identifies E as correct. The first immunoglobulin produced on initial exposure to an immunogen is IgM, followed by IgD; mature naive B lymphocytes can express both IgM and IgD through alternative RNA splicing. The patient's acute symptoms after a bee sting are a type I hypersensitivity reaction mediated by preformed IgE already bound to mast-cell receptors; IgE is not produced as the first antibody during that symptomatic reaction. IgA, IgE, and IgG are produced after the primary IgM response. The source's comparison table notes that the primary response has a 5–10 day lag, a smaller peak, and IgM followed by IgG, whereas a secondary response has a 1–3 day lag and increasing IgG, IgA, or IgE with higher affinity.

stem: A 55-year-old woman comes to the physician because of progressive weakness and fatigue. She also states that she has had dizziness, irritability, and difficulty sleeping for the past 2 months. A complete blood count shows a WBC of 10,000/mm³, hemoglobin of 6.0 g/dL, hematocrit of 18.5%, and platelets of 300,000/mm³. Which of the following sets of changes is most likely to be seen during resting conditions compared to a normal individual?

options.text: Heart rate ↓; stroke volume ↓; cardiac output ↓; pulse pressure ↓
Heart rate ↓; stroke volume ↑; cardiac output ↑; pulse pressure ↑
Heart rate ↔; stroke volume ↔; cardiac output ↔; pulse pressure ↔
Heart rate ↑; stroke volume ↑; cardiac output ↑; pulse pressure ↑
Heart rate ↑; stroke volume ↔; cardiac output ↑; pulse pressure ↔

answer_text: D
explanation: The source states that the patient is severely anemic and that severe anemia may cause high-output cardiac failure. Decreased blood viscosity and peripheral vasodilation (including increased nitric oxide activity) lower peripheral vascular resistance. Cardiac output rises to maintain blood pressure and oxygen delivery, through compensatory increases in resting heart rate and stroke volume; the increase in stroke volume widens pulse pressure. The source gives the relationship P (pressure) = Q (flow/cardiac output) × R (resistance), and lists other causes of high-output failure including sepsis, anaphylaxis, hyperthyroidism, thiamine deficiency, carcinoid syndrome, obesity, pregnancy, systemic arteriovenous fistulas, and Paget disease of bone.

stem: A 48-year-old woman has a 2-year history of joint pain, oral swelling, dry mouth, dysphagia, and new dental caries. She reports adequate hydration and dental hygiene. Her family history is significant for hypertension and rheumatoid arthritis. Physical examination shows slight enlargement of the parotid glands. Laboratory studies show antibodies against ribonucleoprotein antigens. Which of the following would most likely be present in this patient?
answer_text: C
explanation: The source identifies Sjögren syndrome, an autoimmune disease that destroys lacrimal and salivary glands, causing dry eyes, xerostomia, dental caries, and dysphagia. The expected finding is keratoconjunctivitis. Anti-Ro (SS-A) and anti-La (SS-B) antibodies are diagnostic; inflammatory arthritis or concurrent rheumatoid arthritis may occur. The source notes marginal-zone lymphoma in salivary glands as the most serious complication (approximately 5% of patients). Goiter is not typical; although autoimmune thyroiditis can coexist, ocular involvement is more characteristic. Hemolytic anemia is not characteristic. Proximal muscle weakness suggests polymyositis or dermatomyositis rather than this presentation. Urethritis is associated with reactive arthritis, not Sjögren syndrome.

stem: A 29-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 3-week history of swollen and painful knees and toes. He also has some low back stiffness that is worse in the morning and he has been treated recently for conjunctivitis. He also describes an onset of urgency, clear urethral discharge, and dysuria, which started five weeks ago. He is sexually active and has a monogamous relationship with the same person for the past 2 years. His temperature is 37.2°C (99.0°F), pulse is 76/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 128/74 mm Hg. Gram stain of penile discharge is negative for pathogens. Which of the following is most likely to be found in this patient's history?
answer_text: B
explanation: The source identifies reactive arthritis (formerly Reiter syndrome): acute, usually asymmetric arthritis of lower-extremity joints with conjunctivitis and urethritis; diarrhea may precede it. Campylobacter jejuni is one of the triggering microorganisms (along with Shigella, Salmonella, Yersinia, and Chlamydia trachomatis). The source explains that Borrelia causes Lyme arthritis without the conjunctivitis/urethritis pattern; EBV is discussed in relation to rheumatoid arthritis; hyperuricemia predisposes to gout; and gonococcal septic arthritis generally has a different presentation. A negative pathogen Gram stain with clear urethral discharge supports nongonococcal urethritis.

stem: A 19-year-old man comes to the physician because of a seven-day history of weakness, malaise, and a dry cough. His temperature is 38.0°C (100.0°F). A bronchoalveolar lavage is performed and the washings show ‘slow-growing’ organisms on sterol-containing media. Laboratory studies of serum show the presence of cold agglutinins. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?
answer_text: C
explanation: The source identifies primary atypical pneumonia due to Mycoplasma pneumoniae. It is a fastidious extracellular prokaryote without a cell wall and has sterols in its membrane; it grows slowly on sterol-containing media. Infection can produce cold hemagglutinins and Streptococcus MG agglutinins. Treatment is with macrolides; beta-lactams are ineffective because the organism lacks a cell wall. The source contrasts this with routine-culture Klebsiella, Legionella requiring cysteine and iron, parainfluenza causing croup, and typical pneumococcal pneumonia.

stem: A 27-year-old man who is a football coach at a middle school has a history of sickle cell anemia. He notices that one of his players develops a red rash on his cheeks. Two days later, the rash spreads to the student's shoulders, upper chest, and upper arms with a blotchy, net-like appearance. If the teacher becomes infected, he is most likely at increased risk of developing which of the following?
answer_text: B
explanation: The source identifies the student's illness as fifth disease (erythema infectiosum), caused by parvovirus B19. In a patient with sickle-cell anemia, parvovirus infection can cause an aplastic crisis by affecting erythroid precursors and producing pure red-cell aplasia. The source distinguishes this from acute chest syndrome, hemolysis, priapism, and stroke, which are associated with sickling/vascular occlusion rather than the parvovirus-related marrow suppression described.

stem: A 38-year-old man comes to the physician because of a severe rash that involves most of his body, including a maculopapular rash on his palms and soles. His temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse is 78/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 135/90 mm Hg. The patient recalls having a painless lesion on his penis several months ago. He also says that he has occasionally had unprotected sexual intercourse during his travels to Southeast Asia and several US states. Which of the following is the most likely causal agent of this disease?

options.text: Intracellular prokaryote that elicits the Weil-Felix reaction
Single-stranded, positive-sense RNA virus that is diploid
Single-stranded, positive-sense RNA virus that is naked and icosahedral

answer_text: E
explanation: The source identifies secondary syphilis caused by Treponema pallidum. A diffuse rash involving palms and soles following a painless chancre is characteristic. T. pallidum is a thin spirochete (spirillar bacterium) motile by an internal flagellum/axial filament. The distractors describe Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Rickettsia, a retrovirus such as HIV, and a picornavirus such as coxsackie A, respectively; the latter patterns do not fit this presentation.

stem: A 72-year-old man is admitted to the intensive care unit because of multiple medical problems for which he is receiving several different medications. Four days after admission, he develops upper abdominal pain that worsens following a meal. Physical examination shows mild epigastric tenderness. A Helicobacter pylori breath test is negative. Treatment is begun with a negatively charged agent that forms a physical barrier against acid and pepsin. Which drug is most likely?
answer_text: F
explanation: The source identifies sucralfate (aluminum sucrose sulfate). In the acidic stomach it polymerizes and binds exposed positively charged proteins at the ulcer base, forming a protective barrier against acid and pepsin and aiding healing; it can also inhibit pepsin and bind bile salts. The explanation discusses stress ulcers and other ulcer therapies. The distractors are a mucolytic/acetaminophen antidote (acetylcysteine), dopamine-antagonist prokinetic/antiemetic (metoclopramide), PGE1 agonist (misoprostol), proton pump inhibitor (pantoprazole), and H2 antagonist (ranitidine).

stem: A 25-year-old man who is a farmer is brought to the emergency department by his mother because of respiratory distress. After work he began to feel sweaty and dizzy. His pulse is 48/min and blood pressure is 110/72 mm Hg. He appears agitated, is drooling and gasping for air, and his pupils are 2 mm and constrict to light. The toxin to which he was most likely exposed directly interferes with which of the following?
answer_text: A
explanation: The source identifies organophosphate insecticide exposure with acetylcholinesterase inhibition. This raises acetylcholine at synapses and produces excessive muscarinic and nicotinic stimulation, including miosis, bradycardia, bronchospasm, increased GI activity, secretions, and sweating. Treatment includes atropine for muscarinic effects and pralidoxime (2-PAM) to reactivate acetylcholinesterase before enzyme aging. The receptors themselves are not directly inhibited by organophosphates.

stem: Drugs Y and X are infused into an experimental animal and their effects on systemic vascular resistance (SVR) and heart rate (HR) are measured. The experiment is completed over 10 minutes; assume the antagonist (drug Y) persists throughout. The graph shows that after Y, SVR decreases and HR increases; after X, HR increases further while SVR does not change. Which are the most likely identities of Y and X?
answer_text: C
explanation: The source states that drug Y must be phentolamine: alpha-adrenergic blockade lowers SVR and evokes reflex tachycardia, whereas propranolol would block cardiac beta-1 receptors and lower HR. With alpha receptors blocked, norepinephrine's alpha-mediated vascular effect is removed while its beta-1 cardiac stimulation raises HR without changing SVR, matching the trace. Epinephrine or isoproterenol would also stimulate beta-2 receptors and lower SVR, so choices A and B do not fit.

stem: A 57-year-old man with type 1 diabetes mellitus is brought to the emergency department because of severe diarrhea for 4 days. Laboratory studies show pH 7.29, HCO₃⁻ 20 mEq/L, Na⁺ 136 mEq/L, K⁺ 3.2 mEq/L, Cl⁻ 105 mEq/L, and urine pH 5.1. Which of the following would most likely increase urine pH but worsen hypokalemia and acidosis?
answer_text: A
explanation: The source identifies acetazolamide, a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor. The patient has a normal-anion-gap metabolic acidosis (anion gap = 136 − (105 + 20) = 11 mEq/L). Acetazolamide increases urinary bicarbonate excretion, raises urine pH, and can cause/worsen metabolic acidosis and hypokalemia through increased distal sodium delivery and potassium excretion. Ammonium chloride acidifies urine; bicarbonate and loop diuretics tend toward alkalosis; withholding insulin can worsen ketoacidosis but would not be expected to worsen hypokalemia in the way described.

stem: A physician prescribes furosemide for one of the nurses in his office. The next day, the physician receives a call from the local pharmacy informing him that this medication is likely to cause an allergic reaction in the nurse because the pharmacy records indicate that she has a hypersensitivity to sulfa-containing drugs. Which of the following was most likely performed by the pharmacist prior to calling the physician?
answer_text: B. Drug utilization review (DUR)
explanation: Drug utilization review (DUR) is an authorized, organized, continual review of prescribing, dispensing, and use of medication. A DUR incorporates a drug review alongside a predetermined set of parameters that results in changes to both new and existing drug therapy when these criteria are not met. DUR involves comprehensive review of patients’ prescription and medication information before, during, and after dispensing to ensure appropriate medication decision-making and positive patient outcomes. It attempts to identify inappropriate medication use, including therapeutic duplication, drug-drug interactions, drug-disease interactions, improper dosage, and improper treatment durations. Here, pharmacy personnel performed the DUR before dispensing, preventing a potential serious adverse event. AHA/JSA are workplace hazard/risk-assessment tools; FMEA is a prospective process-failure analysis; RCA is retrospective problem solving to identify root causes after a fault or adverse event has occurred.

stem: Anew intern who is not being supervised is asked to see a patient who is being discharged following treatment of a lower extremity deep vein thrombosis. The intern prescribes a 6-month course of warfarin without reviewing the patient’ other medications. Unknown to the intern, the patient i taking an antibiotic which increases the anticoagulant activity of warfarin. The pharmacy computer system is broken and the drug is filled ‘manually which does not enable the computer system to alert to the drug- drug interaction. An overworked nurse fails to check for drug interactions during the medication reconciliation and gives the patient the prescription upon discharge. The patient fills the prescription at a local drug store and suffers a significant bleeding complication requiring re-hospitalization and surgery: According to James Reason's Swiss cheese model of error, which one of the following would be the most effective approach to preventing this adverse event in the future?

options.text: Identifying and correcting the single overarching failure in the health
Identifying and weeding out the individuals involved in this medical
Applying a systemic approach to eliminating all causes of human
Building successive layers of safety barriers into the system that pre-
Initiating a campaign to remind clinicians to be more vigilant and to

explanation:
2. Answer: D. The most effective approach to improving patient safety and
quality is to address system-level causes of failure. In the Swiss cheese
model, safety barriers are recognized as having unintended weaknesses
(i.e, holes) which can occasionally align and allow an error to result in
patient harm. In order to improve patient safety; the system must be rede-
signed to have effective safety barriers capable of preventing errors from
resulting in patient harm. Attempting to penalize individuals who make
honest errors or eliminate the potential for human error yields limited
results,

stem: A23-year-old man with a history of depression is admitted to the inpatient psychiatry ward after the third attempt at suicide with an intentional drug overdose. The patient has been stabilized medically; however, is under 24-hour monitoring by the nursing staff due to repeated attempts at self- harm. During change of shift, there is a mistake in communication and no one is assigned to the patient. The mistake is noticed 15 minutes into the new shift, and a member of the nursing team is assigned to watch the patient. Fortunately, during the 15-minute period the patient did not make any attempts to harm himself. Which of the following statements about this event is correct?

options.text: This is a sentinel event and should be reported to the medical board.
This is a sentinel event and should be reported to the hospital and
This is a near miss and should be reported to the hospital.
This is a near miss and should be reported to the patient and family.
This is a near miss and no reporting is required since the patient was

explanation:
4. Answer: C. The event described is a near miss; there was an error which
fortunately did not result in patient harm. Most near misses need not be
disclosed to patients or families; however, they should be reported to the
hospital in order for the error to be studied in an attempt to learn how to
prevent it in the future. A sentinel event is an adverse event resulting in
Serious or permanent injury to a patient.

stem: A nurse practitioner receives a phone call from the mother of one of the pediatric patients in the practice who frequently suffers from ear infec- tions. The mother typically sees the physician and receives antibiotics to treat her childs condition. Given that it is a weekend and the office is closed, the nurse practitioner phones in the antibiotic prescription based on the mother’s recollection of the name of the medication used in the past. The prescription is filled at a new pharmacy that does not have the patient's prior medical records on file. The child suffers an allergic reaction after which it is discovered that the wrong antibiotic was ordered. Which of the following statements is correct regarding root cause analysis (RCA)?

options.text: RCA involves a retrospective, systems approach to error analysis
RCA is a prospective approach to systems redesign.
RCA involves only the individual(s) directly involved in the error.
RCA is only performed for errors resulting in patient death
Due to privacy laws the results of RCA are confidential and not

explanation:
5. Answer: A. The root cause analysis is a retrospective approach to error
analysis. It is typically performed for errors resulting in significant patient
harm, but can be performed for any adverse event that a team wishes to
review. The RCA process usually involves the individual(s) involved in
the event as well as any other members of the team typically involved
in the care delivery process related to the event. Although the details
such as the names of the individuals involved in the event are not shared
publicly; the general findings of the RCA can be shared throughout the
system in order to improve the quality of the system.

stem: A critical and respiratory care unt is attempting to decrease their rate of ventilator-acquired pneumonia. The team develops a new clinical protocol to help reduce hospital-acquired pneumonia in ventilated patients. The protocol includes several new activities which have not previously been followed uniformly in the unit. The changes includes head of bed eleva- tion, daily oral care, daily assessment of readiness to extubate and having access to infectious disease specialists for consultation in the treatment of ventilator-associated pneumonia. Which one of the following represents an outcomes measure of quality?

options.text: Measure the compliance rate in following guidelines for head of bed
Determine the number of infectious disease specialists available for
Monitor the number of patients who self extubate prematurely dur-
Monitor the number of infections over three months following imple-
Determine the wait time for starting antibiotics in patients with sus-

explanation:
6. Answer: D. The number of infections over 3 months following imple-
‘mentation of the new protocol is an outcomes measure. Compliance rates
in following guidelines are a process measure. The number of infectious
disease specialists would be a structure measure. The number of patients
prematurely self-extubating would be a balancing measure. Wait times for
starting antibiotics is another process measure.

stem: A geriatric team is interested in decreasing the number of patient falls in their nursing home. After convening as a group to discuss possible inter- ventions, a new system of identifying patients at high risk for falling and providing these patients with fll prevention interventions is implemented. Following this intervention, the rate of patient falls per month is followed for 12 months on a run chart. No baseline data was collected. Which of the following best describes the results of the run chart?

options.text: The intervention led to a significant decrease in patient falls
The intervention led to a significant increase in patient falls.
The intervention resulted in no change in patient fll.
The impact of the intervention is subjective
The impact of the intervention is inconclusive

explanation:
7. Answer: E. A run chart provides a dynamic display of a process over
time. Run charts help to determine using minimal mathematical com.
plexity if interventions made in a process or system over time lead to
improvements. Run charts also provide the foundation for the more
sophisticated method of statistical analysis using control charts. The run
chart allows a team to understand the stability of a process as well as
determine any shifts, trends or runs which may indicate changes based on
interventions. However, without a baseline for comparison, one cannot
determine from this run chart whether or not any significant change has
occurred.

stem: a 28-year-old man. The mitral valve in the photograph shows morphologic changes resulting from myxoid degeneration of valve leaflets. Biochemical studies confirm a defect in fibrillin. Patients with this condition are at increased risk for developing which of the following?

options.text: Infarct and rupture of the ventricular wall

answer_text: A
explanation: The source identifies mitral valve prolapse with myxoid mucopolysaccharide accumulation as a feature of Marfan syndrome, caused by an autosomal dominant fibrillin defect. Other features include long limbs/fingers (arachnodactyly), ectopia lentis, and dissecting aortic aneurysm; therefore aortic dissection is the serious increased risk. Atrial fibrillation can rarely occur with mitral regurgitation but is less concerning. Ventricular wall rupture follows myocardial infarction; Libman-Sacks endocarditis is associated with lupus/antiphospholipid syndrome; right ventricular failure is not a specific Marfan risk.

stem: A 59-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of dizziness and confusion. He has a 10-year history of hypertension and a 30-year history of alcohol abuse. He was last seen by a physician 3 years ago. His blood pressure is 178/108 mm Hg. He has not been taking antihypertensive medication or adhering to dietary recommendations since his last office visit. Which of the following is most likely to be increased in his cerebral circulation?
answer_text: B
explanation: The source explains that untreated hypertension causes vascular remodeling, including hypertrophy of arteries and arterioles. Vessel walls thicken and the wall-to-lumen ratio increases, usually narrowing the lumen and increasing resistance; this contributes to ischemia and organ damage. Arteriolar and capillary densities, and their total cross-sectional areas, tend to decrease. The thickened cerebral vessel walls are an adaptation to chronic high pressure.

stem: An investigator uses RFLP analysis with Southern blotting to identify a point mutation in codon 408 of the LDL receptor gene after amplification of exon 9 using PCR. The mutation changes GTG (Val) to GTA (Met) and introduces the stated restriction-enzyme recognition palindrome GTAC, which is absent from the normal exon. The normal amplified exon is 222 base pairs; digestion of the mutant exon produces 126-bp and 96-bp fragments. After digestion and Southern blotting with a probe directed against the entire amplified region, which lane best represents a patient heterozygous for this mutation?
answer_text: C
explanation: A heterozygote has one normal allele and one mutant allele. The normal 222-bp fragment remains intact, while the mutant allele is cut into 126-bp and 96-bp fragments (which sum to 222 bp), yielding three bands in total; lane 3 is correct. Lane 1 (one 222-bp band) represents homozygous normal; lane 2 (126- and 96-bp bands) represents homozygous mutant. A 444-bp band cannot be generated by digestion (lane 4), and lane 5 lacks the expected additional 126- and/or 222-bp fragments. This technique is restriction fragment length polymorphism (RFLP) analysis.

stem: A 13-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her mother because of lethargy and pronounced inactivity. Physical examination shows akinesia and rigidity. A photograph of her eye is shown. Laboratory studies show AST of 136 U/L and ALT of 142 U/L. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy for this patient?
answer_text: E
explanation: The source identifies Wilson disease, an autosomal recessive ATP7B disorder that impairs biliary copper excretion. Copper accumulation causes hepatic, neurologic (including parkinsonism/rigidity), and psychiatric findings; the eye photograph shows a Kayser-Fleischer ring, and ceruloplasmin is typically low. Copper chelation with penicillamine or trientine is used; oral zinc may be an adjunct. Deferoxamine chelates iron, dimercaprol is used for arsenic/mercury/lead poisoning, EDTA for lead, N-acetylcysteine for acetaminophen toxicity, and succimer for lead/arsenic/mercury toxicity. The source names penicillamine as the correct choice while noting trientine can be a suitable primary therapy, particularly when penicillamine is poorly tolerated or neurologic symptoms are present.

stem: A 60-year-old man comes to the physician because of fatigue and back pain. He has a history of hypertension. Physical examination shows abnormal curvature of the lumbar vertebra and the femur bilaterally. The overlying skin in the affected areas is warm to touch. An x-ray of L1-L4 is shown. Laboratory studies show calcium of 9.1 mg/dL and alkaline phosphatase of 190 U/L. Which of the following best explains the current x-ray findings?
answer_text: E
explanation: The source identifies Paget disease. Increased radiologic density and peripheral sclerosis producing a double-contour or picture-frame appearance reflect excessive bone deposition. Paget disease has osteolytic, mixed osteolytic-osteoblastic, and osteoblastic stages; it may cause pain, deformity, neurologic compression, warmth over affected skin, and elevated alkaline phosphatase with normal calcium. The alternatives have different radiographic patterns: fibrous dysplasia causes well-circumscribed radiolucencies; hyperparathyroidism causes cortical thinning; osteomalacia causes decreased bone density/pseudofractures; and osteoporosis causes generalized bone loss and cortical thinning. The x-ray is retained on source page 11.

stem: A 71-year-old man comes to the physician for evaluation of severe COPD. He is a former smoker and works for a fire and water damage restoration company. His wife reports that his mental status has declined over the past few days; he is confused and cannot understand or retain simple information. He is not using oxygen and denies dyspnea, but uses accessory muscles to breathe. Temperature is 37.3°C (99.1°F), pulse 74/min, respirations 19/min, blood pressure 121/69 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 93% on 2 L oxygen. Laboratory studies: Na⁺ 142 mEq/L, K⁺ 4.4 mEq/L, Cl⁻ 89 mEq/L, HCO₃⁻ 44.3 mEq/L, glucose 86 mg/dL, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL, BUN 16 mg/dL, calcium 9.2 mg/dL, pH 7.36. Which is the most likely cause of the altered mental status?
answer_text: B
explanation: The source identifies acute worsening of chronic hypercapnia in severe COPD as the cause. Elevated CO₂ can produce restlessness, confusion, delirium, and tremors; at very high PaCO₂ it can cause CO₂ narcosis. Chronic COPD patients adapt through resetting central chemoreceptor sensitivity and renal bicarbonate retention, so neurologic symptoms may appear when CO₂ rises acutely. The explanation estimates PaCO₂ from the Henderson-Hasselbalch relationship using pH 7.36, bicarbonate 44.3, and pK 6.1, yielding a substantially elevated level. Meningitis is less likely without fever; hypovolemia is unsupported by normal vital signs and renal indices; oxygen saturation is not consistent with hypoxemia; and evidence for commonly encountered mycotoxins causing these symptoms is weak.
